faq.q: Can talking to an AI chatbot make you lonelier?
faq.a: It can, though the effect is small. A 2026 year-long study of 2,149 adults in Psychological Science found that loneliness predicted more social chatbot use four months later, and more chatbot use predicted a small further rise in emotional isolation. The data were self-reported and the authors call the analyses exploratory.

faq.q: Does an AI chatbot help with loneliness at all?
faq.a: In the moment, sometimes. Harvard Business School studies published in 2025 found that an AI companion reduced loneliness right after use, largely by making people feel heard. A 2026 UBC experiment with 296 students found a supportive chatbot lifted mood but did not reduce loneliness over two weeks, while texting a real peer did.

faq.q: Who is most at risk from using AI companions for loneliness?
faq.a: People with small offline social networks who use a chatbot mainly for companionship, use it heavily and disclose a lot to it. A 2026 Nature Human Behaviour study of 1,131 Character.AI users found that combination was associated with lower well-being. The study is correlational, so it can't show the chatbot caused it.

faq.q: How can I use an AI chatbot without it replacing people?
faq.a: Use it to name the feeling, work out which person it is about, and draft a short message to them, then close the app and send it yourself. Ask it to disagree with you rather than agree by default, set a time limit before you start, and check weekly whether you're telling the chatbot things you'd normally tell a person.

faq.q: When should I talk to a professional about loneliness?
faq.a: If loneliness has lasted weeks and comes with low mood most days, trouble sleeping or eating, or losing interest in things, talk to a doctor or counselor. If it comes with hopelessness or thoughts of self-harm, contact a crisis line now; in the US, call or text 988, or call your local emergency number if you're in danger.
